transcript:
Meeting Header: Date: 2026-03-19 14:30 PT. Duration: 64 mins. Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Sana Patel (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Auriga CTO), Maya Rivera (Auriga Head of ML), Ethan Zhang (Auriga Infra). Summary: exploratory discovery about leaving / exiting hosted providers and whether Redwood Hosted/Dedicated/Private fits their regulated workflows; wants parity with OpenAI/Anthropic outputs; asks re: vLLM/TGI compatibility and performance.
00:00 Jordan Park: hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick intros? we'll keep this pretty practical, we mostly want to understand your stack, success criteria, and any blockers for a migration.
00:12 Liam O'Connor: yeah thanks. i'm liam, cto at auriga, we run a clinical decision support product, lots of PHI-ish metadata, so data residency and audit are big. maya runs model dev and ethan runs infra.
00:24 Maya Rivera: hi! we prototype on openai and anthropic for chat/assistant flows, also started some local ops on vLLM for inference microservices.
00:35 Jordan Park: got it. can you share what 'started on vLLM' means—are you running TGI also or is it mostly vLLM? any quantization, 4-bit, etc?
00:44 Maya Rivera: mostly vLLM on our k8s cluster; we tried bitsandbytes 4bit quant for gobbler-llm variant. TGI is an experiment but we hit stability with very long context.. like 8k to 32k tokens with heavy KV churn and the cache invalidation was a pain.
01:03 Sana Patel: that's helpful — the cache/KV behavior is exactly where most migration friction shows up. our runtime supports continuous batching and pinned KV cache strategies; we can emulate your KV eviction pattern in benching. what's your SLOs now for p95 latency and cost per thousand tokens?
01:18 Maya Rivera: p95 is ~220ms on short chit-chat prompts (<=512 tokens) when we use openai gpt-4o-api. for longer threads p95 goes to 1.2s because of attention and KV reads. cost is... we're tracking monthly token spend at about $25k currently.
01:35 Ethan Zhang: and we have strict egress rules; everything must travel over our VPC or be on-prem. SSO via SAML is required, KMS for key material, and we need audit logs with 365 day retention.
01:50 Jordan Park: thanks — that maps cleanly to our offerings. quick mapping: Hosted API — fastest to try but not suitable if you need customer-managed VPC/air‑gapped. Dedicated — reserved GPU pools in our infra, private networking and can route through a peering connection. Private — full VPC control or on-prem for air-gapped. each tier changes routing, SLA, and ability to handle PII/PHI. which of those do you think you need?
02:12 Liam O'Connor: likely Private with VPC or on‑prem because of compliance. but we want to be pragmatic — could we pilot on Dedicated first and then move to Private? need to understand parity of outputs though; the model family must match what we get from OpenAI/Anthropic.
02:28 Sana Patel: absolutely. parity is two parts: model weights/architectural compat (we host vetted open models and can also bring customer-supplied weights), and the runtime differences like tokenizer versions, sampling seeds, and prefix caching. we run deterministic sampling configs and provide seed mapping so you can calibrate.
02:43 Maya Rivera: what about tool-calling and structured JSON outputs, we rely on function calling patterns in openai to drive downstream parsers.
02:50 Jordan Park: we support streaming and function/tool calling. small caveat — sometimes the function schema resolution can be slightly different due to tokenizer byte offsets; we include a utilities library to normalize token offsets and a validation harness for your JSON schema tests.
03:06 Ethan Zhang: network-wise, what does VPC peering look like? we have strict firewall rules and p95 latency goals end-to-end.
03:12 Sana Patel: for Private we do either VPC peering (over cloud providers) or customer-managed VPN / private interconnect. latency will depend on region placement of the inference nodes and your egress. for Dedicated we can colocate the cluster in the same cloud region and offer direct peering — typical additional hop <10ms.
03:30 Maya Rivera: we also care about model tuning — do you support LoRA/Fine-tuning in Dedicated or Private? or is it only hosted fine-tuning?
03:38 Jordan Park: we support fine-tuning and LoRA in Dedicated and Private. hosted has managed fine-tuning but for regulated data we recommend Dedicated/Private so training artifacts don't leave your network.
03:49 Liam O'Connor: how do you handle updates and rollouts — we can't have sudden behavior shifts in prod.
03:54 Sana Patel: rollouts are configurable: canary, A/B, or shadow traffic. we also do automatic fallback to compatible model variants if a newer version crosses quality thresholds. we can hook your eval suites and trigger rollback on regressions.
04:08 Maya Rivera: speaking of evals, we need parity with certain prompts; sometimes OpenAI flattens answers vs Anthropic is more conservative. how do you measure quality and set acceptance?
04:20 Sana Patel: we recommend a three-tier approach: automated metrics (ROUGE/EM/semantic similarity), human evals on a seeded sample, and regression monitoring in prod. we'll run initial parity evals comparing your gold set across our hosted variants and open-source counterparts (and include vLLM/TGI baselines if you want).
04:39 Ethan Zhang: about performance: we've seen vLLM outperform cloud endpoints in cost per token when using aggressive batching, but latency spikes are unpredictable. can Redwood match that economics?
04:50 Jordan Park: depends on workload: continuous batching, prefix caching, and quantization matter. Redwood Optimize can recommend quantization profiles and batching params. Dedicated + automatic batching usually gets most of the cost wins while keeping predictable tail latency.
05:05 Maya Rivera: any known gotchas migrating from TGI specifically? we have some artifacts built on TGI endpoints for text-generation-inference.
05:13 Sana Patel: TGI quirks we've seen: slightly different default temperature/sampling, attention memory handling for very long contexts, and some request/response schema assumptions. we typically do a TGI-compat shim and include small harnesses to map your TGI inputs to our runtime. sometimes tokens end up off-by-one because of tokenizer differences.
05:36 Jordan Park: let me call that out: when customers say 'eval parity' they mean token-level and semantics; we'll do both. first we'll run the same prompts in your current stack (OpenAI/Anthropic/TGI) and in our candidates, collect p50/p95 latency, token cost, and semantic similarity; then review diffs.
05:57 Liam O'Connor: security: SOC2 plus ISO? we need something like that; also, we have a security questionnaire that vendor security sometimes struggles with.
06:05 Jordan Park: we have SOC2 Type II and we're pursuing ISO27001 across key infra teams; i'll include the attestation. we also support SAML/SSO, RBAC, audit logs shipped to your SIEM, and KMS integrations (customer-managed keys) in Private deployments.
06:20 Ethan Zhang: retention controls — can you keep logs within our project for 365 days and ensure purge on request?
06:26 Sana Patel: yes, retention policies are configurable in Private and Dedicated. Hosted has configurable retention windows but for strict legal controls we usually direct customers to Private.
06:34 Maya Rivera: on compute sizing: will you help size GPU pools for us? we have peaks around month ends with batch scoring and streaming interactive traffic daytime.
06:43 Jordan Park: yes, our Dedicated offering has autoscale policies and burst buckets; we'll run a capacity modeling session as part of the pilot. for Private we provide sizing recommendations and optional runbook for ops.
06:57 Liam O'Connor: what's the normal pilot length and criteria to graduate to Dedicated or Private?
07:03 Sana Patel: typical pilot is 2–6 weeks: week 0 install + baseline tests, 1–2 weeks of parity benching, 1–2 weeks of production shadowing. success criteria usually include semantic parity threshold (e.g., >95% pass on gold prompts), p95 latency target, and cost per token within agreed bounds.
07:20 Jordan Park: quick check on paperwork — procurement will need SOW and pricing bands. Jordan to send initial pricing and a sample SOW for Dedicated and Private.
07:29 Maya Rivera: are there references for similar regulated customers?
07:33 Jordan Park: yes, we'll share anonymized case studies and a short 1‑pager on clinical workloads with references to audit and RBAC setups.
07:41 Ethan Zhang: great, let's plan the bench steps: maya will hand over 200 seed prompts and 1GB chat logs; sana to provide scripts and we'll run them both in our vLLM cluster and in Redwood's pilot.
07:50 Jordan Park: perfect. recap next steps: i'll send security docs and pricing, sana will send benchmark plan; liam will share regulatory constraints. schedule infra deep dive.
07:59 Liam O'Connor: thanks team. that was useful.
08:02 Jordan Park: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with the deck and SOW.

Action items (captured): Jordan to send SOC2 attestation + pricing + SOW; Sana to send benchmark harness and sample prompt templates; Auriga (Liam/Maya) to share test prompts, logs, and list of compliance constraints; schedule infra deep dive week of 3/30.
